What should a Spokane seller know about the local housing picture?

Spokane homeowners hold a median home value of $363,500, and 58.8 percent of households own the place they live, according to the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 estimates. The city had an estimated 230,783 residents on July 1, 2025, up 0.8 percent from the April 2020 base.

Spokane sits on the Spokane River in eastern Washington at 1,843 feet above sea level, about 18 miles from the Idaho border and 229 miles east of Seattle. The city covers 60.02 square miles. A citywide median says little about one block, so compare against recent sales on your own street.

How do the 2026 wildfires affect selling a house in Spokane?

They matter a great deal if your house or street was touched. In early August 2026 the Old Trails Fire destroyed more than 600 buildings, which the encyclopedia entry for Spokane calls the worst disaster in the city's history, and the City of Spokane has since run a recovery program for burned and damaged properties.

The city's wildfire information page and the county's recovery pages point owners to several resources:

  • Owners of properties hit by the Old Trails Fire can request an asbestos survey at no cost.
  • Residential applicants for rebuilding permits can use a free application completeness screening from Permavia for one year, which is optional and does not replace the city's own review.
  • The city issued its first rebuild permit after the fires on August 28, 2026.
  • Spokane County publishes a Demolition and Rebuilding FAQ and a Next Steps FAQ for affected owners.
  • Call 311 inside the city, or 509.755.CITY (2489) from outside it, Monday through Friday from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Owners who lost a house or hold a damaged one often weigh rebuilding against selling the lot or the shell. Ask your insurer in writing what a sale does to an open claim before you sign anything, and ask the county assessor how the damage changes your assessed value.

Which Spokane neighborhoods and schools shape what a house is worth?

The answer starts with where the house sits. Downtown and the Riverside neighborhood form the business center, the South Hill rises south of it, and Browne's Addition west of downtown is a National Historic District known for Queen Anne and Craftsman mansions. Hillyard in the northeast began in 1892 as the site of the Great Northern Railway yard. East Central, the University District and West Central round out the older core, and the city counts 18 National Register historic districts. If your home is in one, ask the city's planning staff whether exterior changes need design review before you repaint, re-side or replace windows for a sale.

Most of the city falls within Spokane Public Schools (District 81), the largest public district in the city. The Mead School District serves parts of north Spokane County outside city limits. Gonzaga University, founded in 1887, and Whitworth University, which moved to north Spokane in 1914, are the two best-known campuses in the city.

Jobs follow the same pattern. Education, health care and social assistance employ 26.5 percent of working residents, retail trade 12.7 percent, and the 92d Air Refueling Wing at Fairchild Air Force Base near Airway Heights is the largest military employer. Weather also reaches the house: Spokane averages about 16.5 inches of precipitation a year, 21 days at or above 90 degrees and roughly 2.2 days at or below zero, so roofs, furnaces and insulation get tested at both ends.

What permit steps and city rules come up before a Spokane sale?

Any repair that needed a permit should be closed out with the city before you list. Spokane runs permits through its Accela Citizen Access portal, and the Development Services Center keeps in-person hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday and 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Wednesday. The center is closed on November 26 and 27 for the holiday.

  • Pull permit history for work you did or inherited, such as a finished basement, a new deck or a water heater swap.
  • Ask the permit center how to resolve an open or expired permit before a buyer's inspector finds it.
  • Pay only through the city's portal. The city warns that fake permit invoices are circulating and says it never asks for payment through emailed wire instructions.

The county's parcel information search shows tax history and assessed value for any Spokane parcel, which helps you confirm the lot size and legal description that will go on the deed.

What taxes and paperwork apply when a Spokane house sells?

The seller normally pays Washington's real estate excise tax, and it is due to the county treasurer where the property sits on the date of sale, whether or not the deed has been recorded yet. For Spokane that means the Spokane County Treasurer. The state share is graduated: 1.1 percent on the first $525,000 of the price and 1.28 percent on the slice up to $1,525,000, with the thresholds rising to $551,000 and $1,551,000 for sales that start on January 1, 2027. A local share is added on top, so ask the treasurer for the exact combined rate before you set your net.

Tax not paid within one month of the sale collects interest, which the Department of Revenue lists at 6 percent for 2026. An unpaid tax can also become a lien on the property.

On most house sales you must hand the buyer a completed seller disclosure statement within five business days after both sides sign the purchase contract, and the buyer then has three business days to rescind unless the two of you agree otherwise (RCW 64.06.020). The form asks about structure, roof, systems, smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, and the buyer may waive receiving it. Read the statute and the Department of Revenue's excise tax page before closing.

When does a cash sale make sense for a Spokane house?

A cash sale fits when speed or condition matters more to you than the last few thousand dollars. A listing usually asks for repairs, showings and a financing timeline. A cash buyer takes the house in the shape it is in and can often close on a date you choose, which helps with a fire-damaged home, an inherited house or a rental with a problem tenant.

Before you accept any offer from a Spokane buyer, get these points in writing:

  • The purchase price and who pays the excise tax and recording costs.
  • The closing date and the title or escrow company that will handle it.
  • Whether the buyer will take the house with its repairs, its contents and any open permits.
  • How long the offer stays open and what happens to any earnest money.

Compare that offer with what a listing would net after repairs, commission and carrying costs. If the cash number is lower, the gap is the price of skipping the work and the wait.

More questions about Spokane, WA

How fast can I sell a house in Spokane?

The timeline depends on the route you pick. A cash purchase has no loan approval to wait for, so it can move faster than a listing, but title work and the escrow company set the real closing date.

Who pays the real estate excise tax on a Spokane sale?

The seller usually pays it. It is due to the Spokane County Treasurer on the date of sale, and the state portion is 1.1 percent on the first $525,000 of the price plus a local portion. Ask the treasurer for the combined rate.

Can I sell a fire-damaged house in Spokane?

Yes. Owners affected by the August 2026 Old Trails Fire can request a free asbestos survey from the city, and the county publishes demolition and rebuilding guidance. Talk to your insurer first about how a sale affects an open claim.

Do I have to give a Spokane buyer a seller disclosure statement?

Usually yes. Washington requires a completed form within five business days after the contract is signed on most residential sales, unless the buyer waives it or the transfer is exempt. The buyer then has three business days to rescind.

Where do I check property tax history for a Spokane house?

Use the Spokane County parcel information search, which lists tax history and assessed value. For a payoff or proration at closing, ask the Spokane County Treasurer.

What does the Tacoma housing market look like to a seller?

Tacoma homeowners report a median home value of $479,600 in the Census Bureau's 2020-2024 estimates, and 55.8 percent of households own rather than rent. The city is the county seat of Pierce County and the economic center of the South Sound region, with an estimated 229,816 residents on July 1, 2025.

Which Tacoma neighborhoods do buyers ask about?

Buyers tend to ask which part of town a house is in before anything else. The city is grouped into Central Tacoma, New Tacoma around downtown, North Tacoma, Northeast Tacoma, West Tacoma and the Port of Tacoma area, and each carries its own character.

  • Central Tacoma includes Hilltop, Delong Park, the Wedge, Bryant and College Heights.
  • North Tacoma includes the Proctor District, the North Slope, Old Tacoma, Ruston Way, Skyline and Yakima Hill.
  • West Tacoma includes the Highlands, Narrows, Titlow and Salmon Beach.
  • Downtown takes in the Stadium District, the Theater District, the Dome District and the Thea Foss Waterway.

Transit shapes demand around the core. Sound Transit runs the T Line between Tacoma Dome Station, downtown, the University of Washington Tacoma campus and Hilltop, and also operates Sounder trains and express buses toward Seattle. Most of the city belongs to Tacoma Public Schools, which lists 36 elementary schools, 11 middle schools and 10 high schools, including Stadium High School and Mount Tahoma High School. Ruston is a separately incorporated town and Browns Point is unincorporated, so confirm which jurisdiction your parcel sits in before you ask the City of Tacoma about permits. Tacoma also keeps a historic preservation program with 165 city landmarks and more than 1,000 historic properties across five overlay zones, so ask the city whether your older home sits in one before you plan exterior work.

How do Tacoma's land, water and climate affect a house?

Elevation and shoreline do most of the work. The city ranges from sea level to roughly 500 feet and covers 62.34 square miles, of which 12.62 square miles are water, and it wraps around Commencement Bay on Puget Sound. Many parts of the city have views of Mount Rainier, and the low-lying ground near the Port of Tacoma sits in the path of a lahar from the Puyallup River if the volcano ever erupts.

Tacoma has a warm-summer Mediterranean climate, with July and August the warmest months and December the coldest. Mean daily highs run 48.1 degrees in January and 76.9 in August. The industrial tide flats once produced the odor known as the Tacoma Aroma, which ended when the Simpson Tacoma Kraft mill closed in September 2023.

The Port of Tacoma is among the largest seaports in the Pacific Northwest, and a refinery has operated on the tide flats since 1952. Downtown has been revitalized since the 1990s, with the University of Washington Tacoma campus, the T Line and a restored Thea Foss Waterway. The Tacoma Narrows bridges connect the city to Gig Harbor and the Kitsap Peninsula.

What property maintenance changes are coming for Tacoma owners?

Tacoma adopted a new property maintenance standard that takes effect on January 1, 2027. The City Council passed Ordinance 29125, which brings International Property Maintenance Code standards into the city's Property Maintenance and Nuisance Code and strengthens the tools the city uses against repeat and chronic violations.

The city says it handles roughly 4,500 property maintenance cases a year under older rules in Chapters 8.30 and 2.01 of its code. Section 7 of the ordinance states that the expanded enforcement program becomes operational no earlier than nine months after the council funds it, so the day-to-day effect depends on future budget decisions. If you own a vacant, neglected or rental house in Tacoma, find out whether any open code complaint is attached to it, and read the details at tacoma.gov/IPMC. Ask the city for any open complaint on the property before you list.

What taxes and disclosures come with a Tacoma sale?

Pierce County bills and collects property tax for Tacoma addresses through the Assessor-Treasurer's office at 2401 S. 35th St., Room 142, in Tacoma, reachable at (253) 798-6111. The second-half 2026 payment deadline was November 2, so a closing now should settle any unpaid balance and prorate the part of the year that the buyer will own. Payments can be made online through the parcel search site, by phone at (253) 798-3333, by mail to Pierce County Finance, or at the cashier lobby at 1501 Market St., Suite 120, from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays. Newer exemption rules also matter: starting in January 2027 more Pierce County homeowners who are 61 or older, or who have a qualifying disability, will see their taxes reduced under an expanded state program.

Real estate excise tax is due from the seller at the county treasurer on the date of sale. The state portion is 1.1 percent on the first $525,000 of the price and 1.28 percent on the amount between $525,000 and $1,525,000, and a local portion is added. Under RCW 64.06.020, a seller of most improved residential property must deliver a signed disclosure statement within five business days after the buyer and seller sign a contract. The form includes questions about the roof, plumbing, electrical and heating systems, and it notes that the seller must provide carbon monoxide alarms and at least one smoke detection device.

  • Gather your latest tax statement and any special assessments before listing.
  • Ask the county for the payoff amount on any unpaid taxes.
  • Collect permit records for additions, such as a converted garage or a new bathroom.
  • Check whether the city or the county has any open complaint or lien tied to the parcel.

Should I list my Tacoma house or take a cash offer?

The answer turns on your repair budget, your calendar and how much work the house needs before a buyer's inspector walks through. A listing exposes the house to the open market. A cash offer trades some of that exposure for speed and fewer conditions, which suits a vacant house, an inherited property or a rental with a tenant in place.

Whichever route you choose, compare written offers on net proceeds, not on the headline price. Ask each buyer who pays the excise tax, how long the offer is open, what the closing date is and whether they accept the house as it stands with its contents.

More questions about Tacoma, WA

Can I sell a house in Tacoma that needs repairs?

Yes. A cash buyer may purchase the house as it stands, and on most residential sales you must complete the seller disclosure statement describing the property's condition to the best of your knowledge.

What does Ordinance 29125 mean for Tacoma sellers?

It sets a new property maintenance standard that takes effect January 1, 2027. The expanded enforcement program starts no earlier than nine months after the council funds it, so check for open code complaints on your property before you sell.

Who collects property tax on a Tacoma house?

Pierce County does, through its Assessor-Treasurer's office in Tacoma. Call (253) 798-6111 for assessed values, statements and exemptions, and ask for a payoff figure before closing.

Who pays the excise tax when a Tacoma house sells?

The seller usually pays it, and it is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale. The state rate is graduated, starting at 1.1 percent on the first $525,000, with a local portion added.

How many people live in Tacoma?

The Census Bureau estimates 229,816 residents as of July 1, 2025, up from 219,346 at the April 2020 census. Tacoma is the third most populous city in Washington.

How fast can I sell a house in Vancouver, WA?

The pace of a Vancouver sale depends on the buyer's money, the title work and one county step that every Clark County deed passes through. A buyer who pays cash removes the lender from the timeline, which is why owners facing a move, an inherited house or a repair bill often ask for cash offers. A traditional listing adds showings, an appraisal and a loan approval on top.

Vancouver is the seat of Clark County, on the north bank of the Columbia River directly across from Portland. The Census Bureau puts the population at 199,698 as of July 1, 2025, up 4.6 percent from the 2020 base. That growth means plenty of buyers and plenty of investors looking at the same streets you live on, so comparing more than one offer is realistic here.

What do the numbers say about the Vancouver housing market?

Census data gives a baseline for what a typical Vancouver home looks like on paper. The figures below come from the Census Bureau QuickFacts table for Vancouver city.

MeasureVancouver city
Residents (2025 estimate)199,698
Share of homes lived in by owners50.8%
Median home value$462,400
Median monthly rent$1,702
Households81,504
Average commute23.2 minutes

With 50.8 percent of homes owner-occupied, about half of Vancouver housing is rented. A house that needs work can interest a landlord or investor as much as a buyer who plans to live in it.

Which parts of Vancouver have the oldest housing?

West Vancouver holds downtown and most of the older parts of the city, while East Vancouver grew after the 1997 annexation, which added 11,258 acres and 58,171 residents. NE Andresen Road is the usual dividing line between the two halves.

Several well-known neighborhoods began as wartime housing. When the Kaiser shipyard drew tens of thousands of workers in the 1940s, the Vancouver Housing Authority was created along with six residential developments: Fruit Valley, Fourth Plain Village, Bagley Downs, Ogden Meadows, Burton Homes and McLoughlin Heights. If your house is in one of those areas, expect a buyer's inspector to look closely at age-related items.

  • Original wiring and panels
  • Galvanized or older supply plumbing
  • Foundations, crawl spaces and drainage
  • Roofs and insulation

More than a third of the Vancouver urban area lives in unincorporated pockets such as Hazel Dell, Felida, Orchards and Salmon Creek, which are outside city limits. Find out first whether your address is inside city limits, since the permit and rental rules below apply only there.

How do Vancouver's weather and river affect a house?

Vancouver has a warm-summer Mediterranean climate with about 42 inches of precipitation a year. Rain is frequent from fall through spring and tapers off around mid June, so roofs, gutters and crawl spaces take most of the wear. Cold east winds funnel down the Columbia River Gorge, and the city has seen freezing-rain storms that coat trees and power lines in ice.

The Columbia has flooded the area before, with destructive events in June 1894 and May 1948, though dams have since narrowed the river's swings. Tornadoes have also touched the metro area, including an EF1 that crossed from Vancouver Lake toward Hazel Dell on January 10, 2008. A buyer's inspector will look hardest at the roof, gutters and crawl space, so those are the places to check before you set a price.

What employers, schools and roads matter to Vancouver buyers?

Health care leads local employment. According to the city's 2022 financial report as summarized on Wikipedia, PeaceHealth is the largest employer with 16,500 employees, followed by Vancouver Public Schools, Evergreen Public Schools, The Vancouver Clinic and Battle Ground Public Schools.

Schools are a selling point in two main districts. Vancouver Public Schools covers most of west Vancouver, and Evergreen Public Schools covers most of the east side. Small portions of the city fall in the Camas and Battle Ground districts, so verify the district against your street address.

Commuting shapes demand. Interstates 5 and 205 both cross the Columbia into Portland, SR 14 runs east from downtown, and SR 500 links I-5 to I-205. Rush-hour traffic is heavy on the Interstate Bridge and the Glenn Jackson Bridge, and C-Tran runs local and express bus service. Homes near the freeways often draw commuters who value the shorter trip.

Do I need a permit before selling a Vancouver house?

You need one only if you plan to do the work yourself before closing. The City of Vancouver requires a residential building permit for the construction, alteration, addition, repair or demolition of residential buildings.

The city's residential permit page lists projects that need one:

  • Additions and remodels
  • Adding a garage, carport, deck or patio cover
  • Adding or removing walls
  • Converting a basement, attic or garage into living space
  • Changing the footprint of a structure

Small stand-alone electrical, mechanical or plumbing jobs fall under a trade permit instead. If you suspect past work was done without a permit, the city offers a field evaluation permit, where inspectors decide what permits and corrections are needed. Tree removal also needs a city permit. The Permit Center can be reached at 360-487-7833 for questions.

The city's updated zoning code took effect on July 31, 2026, and it allows more middle housing, up to six units on one lot. A buyer with development plans may value a lot differently than a buyer who wants to move in.

What changes if the Vancouver house is a rental?

Landlords selling in city limits should know about two programs. Since January 1, 2026, owners of residential rentals in Vancouver must register each unit every year, at $30 per unit. The free 90-day window closed on March 31, 2026. Health and safety inspections are planned to begin in mid 2027.

The city's rental registration page covers the sale of a registered rental: the registration must be transferred to the new owner within 60 days of the property transfer, with no extra fee. If you stop renting, you can deregister the property. Questions go to rentalregistration@cityofvancouver.us or 360-487-7928.

Short-term rentals are a separate permit. Vancouver defines one as a rental of fewer than 30 consecutive nights, and the permit requires a Washington business license with the city endorsement, at least $1 million in liability insurance and a notice mailed to abutting neighbors. The city caps total permits at 870, or about 1 percent of its housing stock. A permit does not override a lease or homeowners association rules, so a buyer who plans to use the house this way should confirm the status with the city's short-term rental page.

How do the deed and excise tax work in Clark County?

Every Clark County sale runs through the Treasurer first and the Auditor second. The Treasurer collects the real estate excise tax, and RCW 82.45.090 bars the Auditor from taking a deed for recording until the tax is paid or the Treasurer marks it not due.

The Clark County Treasurer states that the tax is due 30 days from the date of sale and that a $5 processing fee is added. The state part is graduated by sale price:

  • 1.10 percent on a price up to $525,000
  • 1.28 percent from $525,000.01 to $1,525,000
  • 2.75 percent from $1,525,000.01 to $3,025,000
  • 3.00 percent above $3,025,000

A local rate is added on top, so ask the Treasurer or your closing agent for the total on your price. In person, the office is at 1300 Franklin Street, 2nd Floor, Monday to Thursday from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. After payment, the Auditor's Recording Department at the same address records the deed. Its recording guide lists 564-397-2208 for questions.

A third piece of paperwork is the seller disclosure. RCW 64.06.020 sets out the form for improved residential property, and the seller hands it over no later than five business days after a written purchase contract is mutually accepted, unless the parties choose another schedule. A buyer who receives it has a three-business-day window to rescind.

More questions about Vancouver, WA

Can I sell a Vancouver, WA house as-is?

Yes, as-is sales are common. The state's seller disclosure form under RCW 64.06.020 still applies to improved residential property, and unpermitted work you know of belongs on it.

Who records the deed when a Vancouver house sells?

The Clark County Auditor's Recording Department records it, but only after the Treasurer's Office handles the excise tax affidavit. Both offices are at 1300 Franklin Street, and title or escrow companies normally submit the paperwork for you.

What happens to my Vancouver rental registration when I sell?

It transfers to the new owner. The city says the registration must be moved within 60 days of the property transfer, and there is no additional fee. If the buyer will live in the home, the registration can be ended through deregistration.

Does Vancouver cap short-term rental permits?

Yes. The city limits permits to 870, or about 1 percent of its total housing stock. Anyone buying a house to run as a short-term rental should check permit availability with the Permit Center before paying a premium for that use.

Which school district is my Vancouver house in?

Most of west Vancouver is in Vancouver Public Schools and most of east Vancouver is in Evergreen Public Schools. Small portions are in the Camas and Battle Ground districts, so check the address with the district before you describe it to a buyer.

How can I sell my house fast in Yakima, WA?

A sale to a cash buyer is typically the quickest path, since it removes the buyer's mortgage approval and appraisal from the schedule. A listing can still bring a higher price if the house shows well and you can wait for the right offer.

Yakima is the seat of Yakima County and the 11th most populous city in Washington, in the Upper Valley of Yakima County, about 60 miles southeast of Mount Rainier. The Census Bureau estimates 97,458 residents as of July 1, 2025. West Valley and Terrace Heights are unincorporated suburbs that are treated as part of greater Yakima, so confirm whether your address is inside city limits before you check any city rule.

The Yakama people were the first known inhabitants of the valley. The U.S. Army established Fort Simcoe in 1856 after the Yakima War, and Yakima County was created in 1867. The city's name comes from the Yakama Nation, whose reservation lies south of town, and the Yakama Nation's government and enterprises remain among the area's larger employers.

What do Census figures show about Yakima housing?

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table reports the following for Yakima city.

MeasureYakima city
Residents (2025 estimate)97,458

At $297,600, Yakima's median home value is well below Wenatchee's $433,700 and Vancouver's $462,400. About 46 percent of housing units are not owner-occupied, so rentals make up a large part of the local market.

What drives the Yakima housing market?

Agriculture does. The Yakima Valley produces apples, peaches, pears, cherries and melons, along with peppers, corn and beans, and as of 2011 it grew 77 percent of the hops harvested in the United States. Many residents came to the valley to pick, process, market and support that farm economy.

The city's 2022 financial report, summarized on Wikipedia, lists the largest employers:

  • Yakima Valley Memorial Hospital, 2,500 employees
  • Walmart (Yakima, Sunnyside and Grandview), 1,700
  • Yakima School District, 1,594
  • Zirkle Fruit and Washington Fruit and Produce, 1,500 each
  • Yakama Nation Government Operations, 1,289

Downtown Yakima was long the retail hub, but the regional retail core has moved to Union Gap, where a renovated mall and new stores opened.

How does Yakima's climate affect a house?

Yakima has a cold semi-arid climate, with a location in a rain shadow that holds precipitation to about 8 inches a year. Annual snowfall averages 21.6 inches, mostly in December and January, and the average last freeze of spring comes on May 13, with the first freeze of fall around September 30.

Summers are hot. The city averages 40.2 afternoons a year at 90 degrees or higher and 5.7 at 100 degrees or higher, and it reached 113 degrees on June 29, 2021. Day-to-night swings in July average nearly 35 degrees. Roofing, attic insulation, cooling equipment and exterior paint carry the load from those swings, so any receipts or warranties for them are worth collecting before you list. Yakima sits at 1,095 feet above sea level.

Which schools and highways matter to Yakima buyers?

The Yakima School District runs four high schools in the city: Davis High School, Eisenhower High School, Stanton Academy and Yakima Online High School. West Valley High School is in the West Valley School District, and East Valley High School, just east of Terrace Heights, is in the East Valley School District.

Interstate 82 is the main freeway, linking Yakima to Ellensburg and the Tri-Cities with onward routes to Seattle and Oregon. U.S. Route 12 crosses the north of the city and joins I-82 and U.S. Route 97 on the east side. State Route 24 ends in Yakima and leads to Moxee and the farm areas to the east, while State Route 821 follows the Yakima River canyon toward Ellensburg. The average commute for city workers is 17.8 minutes.

Which repairs need a permit in Yakima?

The city's Code Administration office explains this on its permit process page. Some jobs can be applied for online without plan review:

  • Same-for-same plumbing and mechanical change-outs
  • Residential reroofs that are tear off and reroof only
  • Water and sewer line replacements
  • Residential re-siding
  • Oil tank abandonment and removal
  • Woodstove or wood-burning device installation

A remodel needs a building permit application plus plans showing existing and proposed floor plans and wall details. Land use review may be needed first, and the building permit is not issued until it is approved. Electrical permits go through the state Department of Labor and Industries, at (509) 454-3700 for the Yakima office. Questions about the process go to codes@yakimawa.gov or (509) 575-6126, and applications run through buildingyakima.com.

What if my Yakima house is vacant or in poor shape?

The city responds to complaints about conditions on private property, including garbage, overgrown yards, junk vehicles and vacant buildings that are open to unauthorized entry. In March 2024 the City Council adopted the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code, with local changes, as YMC Chapter 11.40.

The Code Compliance page says anyone directly affected by a notice or order can appeal to the hearing examiner, provided a written appeal is filed within 20 days after service. Reports and questions go through the Yak Back portal or the hotline at (509) 576-6657. If you inherited a vacant house and have not yet secured it, securing it early gives you more options with a buyer, whether that buyer is a family or an investor planning a rehab.

How does a deed transfer work in Yakima County?

Yakima County splits the job between two offices. According to the county's property transfer page, every transfer of real property needs a Real Estate Excise Tax Affidavit processed through the County Treasurer's Office with the conveyance document. The Auditor's Recording Division then records the document. Excise tax and transfer fees must be paid in cash or certified funds.

The same order applies statewide under RCW 82.45.090, which keeps the auditor from recording a deed ahead of the tax payment or a not-due notation. Ask the Yakima County Treasurer for the amount that applies at your price, since it includes both a state and a local portion.

A mobile home follows a different path. If the sale does not require moving it, a Mobile Home Real Estate Excise Tax Affidavit is used, and the Auditor's Vehicle Licensing Division handles the new owner's title. Property taxes must be paid in full before that processing. For a house, the seller also fills out the condition form from RCW 64.06.020 and gives it to the buyer shortly after contract, five business days being the default limit.

More questions about Yakima, WA

Can I sell a Yakima house with an old roof or siding?

Yes. Plenty of buyers take older roofs and siding as they are. If you decide to fix the roof or siding first, the city lets residential reroofs (tear off and reroof only) and re-siding be applied for online without plan review.

What payment form does Yakima County accept for excise tax?

Cash or certified funds. The county's property transfer page states that excise tax and transfer fees must be paid in cash or certified funds.

Can I appeal a city notice about my Yakima property?

Yes. Anyone directly affected by a property maintenance decision, notice or order may appeal to the hearing examiner. The written appeal must be filed within 20 days after the notice is served.

Where do I get an electrical permit in Yakima?

Electrical permits and inspections come from the state Department of Labor and Industries, not the city. The Yakima office is at 15 W Yakima Ave., Suite 100, and the phone number is (509) 454-3700.

Is my house in the Yakima School District?

It depends on the address. The Yakima School District runs Davis, Eisenhower, Stanton Academy and Yakima Online, while West Valley and East Valley are separate districts. Call the district office to verify the boundaries for your street.

How do you sell a house fast in Kirkland, WA?

A Kirkland owner has three routes: list with an agent, sell without one, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who pays without a mortgage. The cash route removes loan approval and usually the repair list, which is why it is the quickest of the three. Every route still ends at the same Washington closing items: excise tax, prorated property tax and a completed seller disclosure statement.

Kirkland is an expensive place to own a home, and that shapes the decision. The Census Bureau reports a median value of owner-occupied housing of $1,115,400 for 2020 to 2024, with 60.8 percent of homes owner-occupied. At those values, the graduated state excise tax and the carrying cost of an empty house both matter, so a shorter timeline can be worth real money.

What is Kirkland like for a home seller?

Kirkland sits on the eastern shore of Lake Washington, and its downtown wraps around Moss Bay with restaurants, galleries, parks and a large stock of condominiums built since the 1990s. Interstate 405 links it to Bellevue, Renton and Bothell, and State Route 520 reaches Seattle and Redmond. The city covers 17.81 square miles of land and ranges from 14 to 500 feet above sea level.

The city was incorporated in 1905, merged with the neighboring town of Houghton in 1968, and grew through annexations. Totem Lake joined in 1974, South Juanita and the Rose Hill areas in 1988, and Finn Hill, North Juanita and Kingsgate on June 1, 2011, which added about 33,000 residents. A house in one of those areas can have a very different lot, age and street pattern from one near Moss Bay, so a buyer or appraiser will compare it against its own neighborhood.

  • Moss Bay and downtown: condominiums, apartments and the waterfront.
  • Houghton: where the first homesteads went up in the late 1860s.
  • Rose Hill: the hill where a steel mill was finished in 1892, with North and South Rose Hill annexed in 1988.
  • Totem Lake: annexed in 1974 and served by Sound Transit and Community Transit buses on I-405.
  • Juanita, Finn Hill and Kingsgate: the northern neighborhoods, with Finn Hill, North Juanita and Kingsgate annexed in 2011.

Most of Kirkland is in the Lake Washington School District, with Juanita High School and Lake Washington High School inside the city. Smaller parts fall in the Bellevue and Northshore districts. Evergreen Healthcare, Google and the school district were the three largest local employers in 2023.

What taxes and fees does a Kirkland seller pay at closing?

The seller normally pays Washington real estate excise tax, and it is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale. The Department of Revenue says an unpaid tax can become a lien on the property, and interest runs if it is not paid within one month of the sale date. A local excise tax set by the city is added to the state portion, so ask your escrow officer for the combined figure on your parcel.

The state portion is graduated under RCW 82.45.060. The Department of Revenue lists these thresholds for sales beginning January 1, 2027:

  • 1.1 percent on the part of the price up to $551,000.
  • 1.28 percent on the part from $551,000 to $1,551,000.
  • 2.75 percent on the part from $1,551,000 to $3,051,000.
  • 3 percent on anything above $3,051,000.

As an illustration, a $1,200,000 sale closing in 2027 would owe $6,061 on the first slice and $8,307 on the next $649,000, about $14,368 in state tax before the local portion. Sales that close before January 1, 2027 use the earlier thresholds, which your escrow officer will apply. Details are on the Department of Revenue excise tax page.

When are King County property taxes due on a Kirkland home?

King County property tax is due in two halves, on April 30 and October 31. The second-half 2026 date has already passed, and the next first-half payment is due April 30, 2027. The King County Treasury takes payment online, by mail with a postmark on or before the due date, in person at 201 S. Jackson Street in Seattle, or at a drop box at the same building.

When a Kirkland house sells mid-year, the escrow officer prorates the bill between you and the buyer, so confirm that your last payment has posted before closing. The Treasury has posted a notice that processing of some second-half 2026 payments was delayed, and it asks owners to check the online portal to confirm their account was credited. Seniors, people with disabilities and some disabled veterans may qualify for exemption or deferral programs, which the King County Assessor administers.

Can you sell a Kirkland house that has tenants or a short-term rental license?

Yes, but Kirkland treats rentals as a business activity. The city requires a business license for any long-term or short-term rental, and operating without one can be a misdemeanor. A buyer who plans to keep the rental will ask for the license history, so have it ready.

Short-term rentals (under 30 days) fall under Ordinance O-4607, and the city's page lists the main limits for single-family homes:

  • An owner or agent who lives in the home continuously may rent short-term with no day cap, up to two rentals at a time.
  • An owner or agent present at least 245 days a year may rent short-term up to 120 days a year.
  • When no one is home, a property manager within 15 miles must be named to the city.
  • Parking is one stall per rental, plus two more stalls if permanent residents live in the home.

The city lists a $100 base fee plus a $130 per-employee regulatory fee for the business license, or $230 for many short-term rentals. Kirkland charges no business and occupation tax. A condominium is generally outside these rules, but the association's own rules still apply. Owners are responsible for lodging tax under state law.

Does Kirkland's weather affect when to sell?

Kirkland averages 36.27 inches of precipitation a year, with the wettest months being November at 5.84 inches, December at 5.43 inches and January at 4.81 inches. Summer is dry, with July averaging 0.79 inches. The record high of 109 degrees came on June 28, 2021, and snow averages 8.1 inches a year.

A winter buyer inspection happens in the wettest weather, so roof, gutter and drainage problems show up quickly. If you are fixing anything, finish those items before listing. If you are selling as-is to a cash buyer, the schedule does not depend on the season.

What must a Kirkland seller disclose?

Washington requires the seller of improved residential property to deliver a completed disclosure statement unless the buyer waives it or the transfer is exempt, under RCW 64.06.020. The form asks about sewer or septic, roof leaks in the last five years, structural issues, and environmental concerns such as lead-based paint or storage tanks. It covers what you actually know, and the buyer has three business days from delivery to rescind unless both sides agree otherwise in writing.

Answer every line, and write NA where a question does not apply. An incomplete form invites disputes later, whether the buyer is financing or paying cash.

More questions about Kirkland, WA

How fast can a Kirkland house sell for cash?

A cash sale can close faster than a financed sale because no lender approval is required, and timing is set by title work and the closing date you choose. The county treasurer must still receive excise tax and the deed must be recorded.

Who pays the real estate excise tax in Kirkland?

The seller usually pays it, according to the Department of Revenue, and if the seller does not, the buyer becomes responsible. The tax is due to the King County treasurer on the date of sale, with interest if unpaid after one month.

Do I need a business license to rent my Kirkland house before selling?

Yes. Kirkland requires a city business license for long-term and short-term rentals, and short-term rentals also need a state license. Operating without one can be a misdemeanor, so settle that before a buyer reviews your rental records.

Are King County property taxes still due if I am selling?

Yes, until closing. Payments are due April 30 and October 31, and the escrow officer prorates the bill at closing. Check the Treasury's online portal to confirm your payment posted.

Can I sell an inherited house in Kirkland?

Yes, it can be sold once the person with legal authority to sign the deed is in place. Ask a Washington estate attorney or your title company who that is, and note that a deed transfer still goes with an excise tax affidavit to the King County treasurer.

What should a seller know about Pasco, Washington?

Pasco is the county seat of Franklin County and one of the three Tri-Cities, with Kennewick and Richland across the Columbia River to the south. The Census Bureau estimates 82,848 residents as of July 1, 2025, up 7.1% from the April 2020 estimates base.

Pasco was incorporated on September 3, 1891, as a Northern Pacific Railway town. Grand Coulee Dam, completed in 1941, brought irrigation to the area and tied the city to farming for decades. The city covers about 34 square miles, roughly 30.5 of them land.

A seller here deals with city hall for permits and rental licenses, with the Franklin County Treasurer for tax and excise payments, and with the Pasco School District for school boundaries that buyers ask about. The rest of this page covers each in turn.

What do the Census numbers say about Pasco homes?

Seven in ten Pasco homes are owner-occupied. The table shows the main figures from Census QuickFacts.

How does Pasco's desert climate affect a house sale?

Pasco sits in the rain shadow of the Cascade Range, so the area is dry and windy. Summers are hot, with a mean daily high of 93.3 degrees in July and a record high of 115 degrees in June, and winters are cold enough to reach a record low of minus 19 degrees in January.

Those swings put a premium on a few items a buyer will check:

  • Air conditioning age and capacity, since cooling runs for months.
  • Roof condition and attic insulation under strong summer sun.
  • Irrigation systems and landscaping that survive on little rain.
  • Pipes and exterior faucets that can freeze in a cold snap.

Service records for the cooling system and roof give a buyer something concrete to review. If a unit is near the end of its life, say so on the disclosure form rather than waiting for the inspector.

What do Pasco schools, jobs and neighborhoods mean for a seller?

The Pasco School District runs the city's public schools. Pasco High School is the older of two long-standing high schools, Chiawana High School opened in August 2009, and a third, Sageview High School, opened in 2025 to relieve crowding at Chiawana. Delta High School, a STEM program shared with the Kennewick and Richland districts, opened in 2015. Columbia Basin College and Washington State University Tri-Cities serve the city's students.

The Census shows 67.0% of residents age 16 and older in the labor force, and Census business data show about $359 million in 2022 transportation and warehousing receipts in Pasco. Mean travel time to work is 22.5 minutes. Buyers who commute across the river to Kennewick or Richland will weigh that against price.

Parts of Pasco are newer subdivisions and parts are older neighborhoods near downtown, so a nearby sale of a similar house is a better guide to price than the citywide median. Ask an agent or your cash buyer which recent sales they used.

Which Pasco city rules matter before you sell?

Pasco's Ordinance No. 4770, adopted June 2, 2025, removed permit requirements for several small jobs. The city's permit page lists them, and they matter if you want to tidy the house before listing:

  • One-story detached sheds or playhouses up to 200 square feet in residential areas.
  • Fences under 7 feet, retaining walls under 4 feet, and decks under 200 square feet and 30 inches high.
  • Residential roofing and siding replacement limited to the shingles, underlayment, flashing, siding, barrier and veneer.

Structural work, anything habitable, and building in an easement or too close to a property line still need a permit. A permit is good for 180 days from issue, and passing an inspection renews that clock, according to the city's ADU guide.

That guide, published in 2023, says Pasco allows one attached or detached ADU per residential parcel, up to 1,000 square feet or 55 percent of the main house, whichever is less. The unit must be long-term housing, with occupants living there more than 180 days a year, and short-term rentals are not allowed. Landlords need a rental business license under PMC 5.60.010. Call Pasco Community and Economic Development at (509) 545-3441 to confirm current rules for your zone.

How is real estate excise tax handled on a Pasco sale?

The seller owes it. RCW 82.45.080 makes the excise tax the seller's obligation. The state portion is 1.1% on the part of the price up to $525,000, then 1.28% to $1,525,000, then 2.75% to $3,025,000 and 3% above that, with the local portion added on top.

At the Census median of $376,300, the state portion alone would be about $4,139. The Department of Revenue moves the thresholds to $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000 for sales beginning January 1, 2027. Ask the Franklin County Treasurer for the local rate.

Payment is due on the date of sale, which is the date the deed is notarized, and the one-month grace period before interest starts runs from that date. You submit the affidavit, the deed and the payment to the county treasurer. If a seller overpays, a refund request must be filed within four years of the sale and the refund goes to the party who paid. The Department of Revenue REET page has the forms.

How do Franklin County property taxes work at closing?

Franklin County's Treasurer says taxes are payable on or after February 15, with the full amount due by April 30. When the bill is more than $50, half can be paid by April 30 and the second half by October 31. The Treasurer is at 1016 N 4th Avenue in Pasco, phone 509-545-3518.

For real property, the Treasurer starts foreclosure action when taxes have been delinquent for three years, so a seller with old arrears should pay them off at closing. Ask your closing officer for a current tax status before you sign.

Owners who are 61 or older, disabled, or disabled veterans may qualify for a deduction, and the Franklin County Assessor handles those applications at 509-545-3506. If you are selling because you can no longer keep up with the house, ask the Assessor whether a reduction would have applied in a prior year.

What options does a Pasco seller have?

A seller can list with an agent, sell without one, or accept an as-is offer from a cash buyer. Each ends with the same deed, affidavit and tax steps, so the choice comes down to timing, condition and price.

  • A listing suits a house in good shape and an owner who can wait through showings and financing.
  • A direct as-is sale suits a house with deferred repairs, a tenant, or an inherited property.
  • Ask any buyer who pays the excise tax, how the date of sale is set, and how back taxes are handled.

More questions about Pasco, WA

How much is the excise tax on a Pasco house sale?

It is 1.1% on the first $525,000 of the price under current state rules, plus a local portion set for Pasco. A $376,300 sale would owe about $4,139 at the state rate. The Franklin County Treasurer can quote the local rate.

When are Franklin County property taxes due?

The full tax is due by April 30, and for bills over $50 you may pay half by April 30 and the second half by October 31. The October 31, 2026 date has passed, so the next deadline is April 30, 2027.

Can I rent out an ADU in Pasco as a vacation rental?

No. The city's ADU guide says an ADU must be used for long-term residential purposes, with occupants living there more than 180 days a year, and short-term rentals are not allowed.

Do I need a permit to replace my roof in Pasco?

Not for a shingle, underlayment and flashing replacement. Ordinance 4770 removed that requirement, but structural roof work still needs a permit.

Who do I call about taxes for a senior or disabled owner in Franklin County?

The Franklin County Assessor at 509-545-3506. The county lists a deduction for owners who are 61 or older, disabled, or disabled veterans.

What are your options for a fast house sale in Marysville, WA?

Marysville owners generally choose among listing with an agent, selling directly to a buyer they find themselves, or taking a cash purchase on the house as it stands. Time is the main variable. A listing needs prep, showings and a financed buyer's loan approval, while a cash sale can compress the schedule when the house has deferred maintenance, a tenant, or a pending deadline.

Marysville is now the second-largest city in Snohomish County, with a Census Bureau estimate of 77,686 residents in July 2025, up 9.9 percent from the April 2020 estimates base.

Whatever route you pick, collect these documents first.

  • The deed and your most recent Snohomish County property tax statement.
  • Payoff letters from your lender and any lienholder.
  • Receipts and permit records for major work, such as a roof, addition or deck.
  • Your completed seller disclosure statement.

What does the Census say about Marysville homes and households?

Marysville is mostly an owner-occupied city with prices below Lynnwood and well above Longview. These figures come from the Census Bureau's QuickFacts for the city.

  • Owner-occupied housing rate, 2020 to 2024: 69.4 percent.
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $567,900.
  • Median monthly owner costs with a mortgage: $2,409.
  • Median gross rent: $1,997.
  • Households: 25,969, averaging 2.79 persons.
  • Median household income: $103,974.
  • Mean travel time to work: 31.5 minutes.

Those numbers describe the whole city, so treat them as background. Your own price depends on the house, its condition and recent sales on your block.

How did Marysville grow, and what does the land look like?

James and Maria Comeford started a trading post here in 1872 on the edge of the Tulalip Indian Reservation. The town was platted on February 25, 1885, and incorporated as a fourth-class city on March 20, 1891, the same year the Great Northern Railway came through. Strawberry fields covered more than 2,000 acres by 1920, which gave Marysville its nickname, Strawberry City, and the Strawberry Festival has been held since 1932.

Growth came in waves. Suburban development began in the 1970s and 1980s, the population grew fivefold between 1980 and 2000, and annexations to the north and east in the early 2000s pushed the city past 20 square miles and 60,000 residents. Marysville runs north to south along Interstate 5, with the Tulalip reservation to the west and State Route 9 to the east.

The terrain matters when you sell. Downtown sits about 5 feet above sea level along Ebey Slough, while the land climbs to about 160 feet near Smokey Point and over 465 feet in the eastern highlands. Two creeks, Quilceda and Allen, drain the area along with roughly 70 smaller streams. If your house is low or near water, ask the county for the flood zone information and a survey so a buyer's lender does not raise it first.

How do commutes and roads affect a Marysville listing?

Most Marysville workers commute out of the city. About 9 percent of residents work inside city limits, roughly 20 percent work in Everett and 13 percent in Seattle, and the average one-way trip is around 32 minutes, with 70 percent driving alone. The Census Bureau lists mean travel time at 31.5 minutes.

Community Transit runs four local bus routes in Marysville and express service from park and ride lots, including all-day service to Lynnwood City Center station and peak service to the Boeing Everett Factory. Marysville sits outside the Sound Transit service area. The state began work in 2023 on a northbound high-occupancy vehicle lane on I-5 and a new interchange at State Route 529, and in 2014 voters approved a 0.2 percent sales tax for city transportation improvements.

Buyers weigh access to I-5 and State Route 529 heavily, so state in plain terms how long your house is from the on-ramp and from Everett.

Which school district serves Marysville?

The Marysville School District covers most of the incorporated city and the Tulalip Indian Reservation, and its high schools are Marysville Pilchuck and Marysville Getchell. Parts of the city fall in the Arlington, Lake Stevens or Lakewood school districts, so a buyer with children will want to confirm the district for your exact address.

What do Marysville permits cost in time, and what rules affect an ADU?

Marysville posts the average staff review time for each permit type. The figures below are calendar days for the first quarter of 2026, drawn from the city's Permit Turnaround page.

Residential permit typeAverage review, days (Q1 2026)

Building permit applications go through the city's online permit portal. Permit questions can go to MSVLPermits@marysvillewa.gov, and planning questions to Planning@marysvillewa.gov. The phone line, 360-363-8000, is staffed from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Accessory dwelling units are a selling point on larger lots. Marysville's ADU guide says a lot may have two ADUs, each between 200 square feet and the greater of 1,000 square feet or 50 percent of the main house, capped at 1,400 square feet, with one parking space per unit and separate water and sewer connections in most cases. The same guide states that short-term rental units are prohibited in the city, so do not market a house or ADU to a buyer as a short-term rental.

To find your zoning, the city publishes a zoning map. For property lines, the city says a licensed survey is the only reliable answer, and recorded surveys can be searched through the Snohomish County Auditor.

What does Washington law require when you sell in Marysville?

Two state rules shape most Marysville closings. First, RCW 64.06.020 requires the seller disclosure statement within five business days of mutual acceptance unless the parties agree otherwise, and the buyer can rescind within three business days after receiving it. Second, the real estate excise tax is due when the sale occurs, usually from the seller.

The Department of Revenue's graduated state rate for sales starting January 1, 2027 is 1.1 percent through $551,000, 1.28 percent through $1,551,000, 2.75 percent through $3,051,000 and 3 percent beyond. Earlier sales use $525,000, $1,525,000 and $3,025,000 as the breakpoints. A local rate is added, so ask the Snohomish County Treasurer for the combined figure on your price. With a city median value of $567,900, a typical Marysville sale crosses into the 1.28 percent band.

How does Snohomish County value and tax a Marysville house?

Snohomish County's assessor must appraise real property at 100 percent of true and fair market value, using a sales comparison, a replacement cost, or an income approach. The county revalues every year as of January 1 and mails the notice in June. The value in that notice is used to calculate the next year's tax.

If you think the number is off, call the assessor's phone number on the notice and ask for an appraiser. The next step is a Board of Equalization petition, which must be filed within 60 days of the mailing or by July 1, whichever is later, and the clerk can be reached at 425-388-3407. The two tax installments are due April 30 and October 31, and a mailed payment must be postmarked by then. Your escrow company will prorate the current bill at closing.

How do you judge a cash offer on a Marysville house?

Judge it by what you keep after all costs. Add up the offer, subtract the payoff and excise tax, and compare the result with the list-price scenario after commission, repair credits and the months of payments you would carry. Ask for the closing date in writing, and have a title company handle the transfer.

More questions about Marysville, WA

How long does a Marysville permit take to review?

It depends on the type. The city's Q1 2026 averages were 8 days for decks, 18 for remodels, 26 for new residential and 34 for accessory dwelling units, counted in calendar days of staff review. Your project may take longer if the city asks for revisions.

Can I use a Marysville ADU as a short-term rental?

No. The city's ADU standards guide says short-term rental units are currently prohibited in Marysville. A buyer who plans nightly rentals would need to look at other options.

What is the deadline to appeal my Snohomish County assessed value?

You must file a completed petition with the Board of Equalization within 60 days of the notice mailing or by July 1, whichever is later. The clerk of the board is at 425-388-3407. You do not need an attorney, but you do need evidence that the value is wrong.

Who pays the Washington excise tax on a house sale?

Usually the seller. The Department of Revenue says the buyer is responsible if the seller does not pay. The tax goes to the county treasurer on the date of sale, and your closing agent normally deducts it from your proceeds.

Do I have to give a Marysville buyer a disclosure statement?

In most sales of improved residential property, yes. RCW 64.06.020 sets the form and the five business day delivery window, and the buyer can rescind within three business days after receiving it. A buyer can waive the right in writing, and some transfers are exempt.

The city also has a registration and inspection program for rentals, covered below, which shapes how a rented house sells.

How did Lakewood become a city, and how is it laid out?

Lakewood was incorporated on February 28, 1996, the same day as Edgewood, after voters had turned down incorporation in 1971, 1990 and 1994. It became the second largest city in Pierce County at once. The city has 17.06 square miles of land and several lakes.

  • American Lake: the largest, at 1,091 acres and an average depth of 53 feet.
  • Lake Steilacoom, Gravelly Lake, Lake Louise and Waughop Lake: the other named lakes, with Waughop Lake inside Fort Steilacoom Park.

State Route 512 ends at its western terminus where it meets Interstate 5 in Lakewood. Pierce Transit is headquartered in the city, and the Lakewood Sounder station, which opened in 2012 as the southern end of the S Line, runs commuter trains north through Tacoma to Seattle. What drives Lakewood's economy and local services?

Joint Base Lewis-McChord, a military installation with about 55,000 employees, sits beside the city, and the local economy is closely tied to it. Lakewood had 30,662 full-time jobs in 2023, with more than 9,000 of them in health care. St. Clare Hospital was the largest employer at 598 employees, and the city recorded $1.65 billion in taxable retail sales in 2022. The Census Bureau counts 6,594 veterans among residents.

Public services are split among several providers, which matters when you fill in disclosure forms or hand over utility accounts:

  • The Clover Park School District runs the public schools for most of the city, and parts of Lakewood sit in the Steilacoom Historical and Tacoma districts.
  • Electricity comes from Lakeview Light and Power on the east side, Tacoma Power on the north side and Puget Sound Energy on the west side, which is also the only natural gas provider.
  • The Lakewood Water District supplies tap water to 17,680 connections.
  • Pierce County Public Works and Utilities maintains sanitary sewer, and the city manages stormwater.
  • The Lakewood Police Department began independent operations on November 1, 2004, and West Pierce Fire and Rescue covers the city.

Which Lakewood landmarks and campuses do buyers recognize?

Fort Steilacoom Park holds Waughop Lake, and Western State Hospital, a 745-bed state psychiatric hospital, stands on the site of the old Fort Steilacoom. Lakewold Gardens, Thornewood, the Lakewood Playhouse (founded 1938) and the Lakewood Towne Center round out the local landmarks. Pierce College Fort Steilacoom and Clover Park Technical College are the two campuses in the city.

Health care includes St. Clare Hospital, which began as Lakewood General Hospital in 1961, and the VA American Lake Medical Center, which opened in 1924 as a veterans hospital. The Pierce County Library System has served Lakewood since the area was annexed in 1996, and its interim library location opened in September 2024.

An initial inspection may be done by a city inspector or by a qualified private inspector, and every re-inspection is done by the city. Inspectors look at structural integrity, weather exposure, plumbing and sanitation, heat and water, ventilation, electrical wiring, exits, and smoke and carbon monoxide detectors.

An owner who fails to register can face penalties under the city's fee schedule and the Lakewood Municipal Code, and a rental business license can be revoked. A buyer of a rented house will ask for registration and inspection records, so gather them before you list. Exemptions under LMC 5.60.025 include:

  • Units occupied by the owner, or by the owner's parent or child.
  • Mobile and manufactured homes, shelters and transitional housing.
  • Condominiums and townhouses in multi-unit structures under multiple ownership, unless one owner holds them.
  • Units built in the past 10 years with a certificate of occupancy and no code violations.

Renting rooms in a home you live in does not require registration, but moving out and renting the whole house does. Contact the program at 253-512-2261 or rentals@cityoflakewood.us.

Short-term rentals of under 30 days are allowed in most zones. The city excludes Commercial 1 to 3, the Industrial Business Park, Industrial 1 and 2, Public and Semi-Public Institutional and Open Space Recreation 1 and 2. A short-term rental must register with the Rental Housing Safety Program, hold a business license, renew annually and be inspected every five years, with a free first inspection. The city handles the permit as a Type II administrative decision. Check your zoning before you promise a buyer short-term rental income.

When are Pierce County property taxes due for a Lakewood house?

Tax statements go out in February. If the amount is more than $50 it may be paid in two installments, April 30 and October 31, and an amount of $50 or less is due in full on April 30. Pierce County says that if a payment envelope is postmarked before the statutory deadline, interest and penalty are waived. October 31, 2026 fell on a Saturday, and the second-half deadline has now passed.

Pay online or at the Assessor-Treasurer's Office, 2401 S. 35th St., Room 142, Tacoma, which also has a drop box. Foreclosure avoidance payments go by cashier's check to that office. For status, call the Assessor-Treasurer hotline at (253) 798-6111. Mortgage companies follow the same payment rules as the owner.

What does a Lakewood seller owe and disclose at closing?

The seller normally pays the state real estate excise tax, which the Department of Revenue says is due on the sale date, and a city local tax is added. The graduated state rate starts at 1.1 percent on the first slice of the price under RCW 82.45.060, and the thresholds change January 1, 2027. On a sale at the $461,200 median value, the first-slice rate would give about $5,073 in state tax before the local portion.

The disclosure form under RCW 64.06.020 asks about the sewer connection, roof leaks and environmental items. The buyer has three business days after delivery to rescind unless the contract provides otherwise.

Registration is required each year while the house is rented, unless an exemption applies. A buyer will want the certificate and inspection history, so register and inspect first if you have not.

Can I sell a Lakewood house with tenants?

Yes. A buyer who keeps the tenant will look at the city's rental registration and inspection records. Ask a Washington attorney how your lease and notice requirements apply.

The first half is due April 30 and the second half October 31, and amounts of $50 or less are due in full on April 30. The next first-half deadline is April 30, 2027.

Yes, in most zones, with a business license, registration in the Rental Housing Safety Program and a permit. Commercial 1 to 3 and several industrial and open space zones are excluded.

Who pays excise tax when a Lakewood house sells?

The seller usually pays, according to the Department of Revenue, and the tax is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale. If it goes unpaid, interest accrues from the sale date.

What are your options for selling a house fast in Lacey, WA?

A Lacey homeowner can list through an agent, sell directly to a buyer found without one, or take an as-is cash offer. A listing gives the widest buyer pool but depends on showings and on a buyer's loan being approved. A cash sale trades some of that reach for a shorter, more predictable path to the closing table.

The Census Bureau puts the median value of owner-occupied homes at $457,100 for 2020 to 2024, and 55.9 percent of homes are owner-occupied. Nearly one in five residents is 65 or older and 6,607 residents are veterans, groups that often face estate, downsizing and relocation decisions.

How is Lacey laid out, and why does it matter to a seller?

Lacey lies between Olympia on the west and the Nisqually River delta on the east. Its northern edge reaches the Nisqually Reach of Puget Sound beside Tolmie State Park, and the BNSF Seattle Subdivision forms much of the southern boundary. The city covers 17.2 square miles of land.

Interstate 5 runs west to east through the middle of the city, so location relative to the freeway affects commute and noise. A few road and transit facts a buyer will weigh:

  • The first diverging diamond interchange in Washington opened in August 2020 where I-5 meets Marvin Road (State Route 510).
  • Intercity Transit runs the county bus system, and Lacey is the eastern end of its bus rapid transit route, The One.
  • Centennial Station, the only Amtrak stop in Thurston County, sits near Lacey's southern edge and sees Cascades and Coast Starlight trains.
  • The city maintained 178.6 miles of streets as of 2021.

The mean commute for Lacey workers is 25.4 minutes, according to the Census Bureau.

What shaped Lacey's history and economy?

Settlers Isaac and Catherine Wood claimed land in 1853 and the place was first called Woodland. When the community applied for a post office in 1891 the name was taken, and Lacey was chosen. Voters rejected incorporation in 1964 and approved it in 1966, and the city was officially incorporated on December 5, 1966.

The South Sound Center opened in 1966 and remains the largest retail area. Lacey designated 500 acres in Hawks Prairie for industrial use in the 1990s, and the area filled with warehouses and distribution centers, including a Target facility of about 1.7 million square feet that opened in 2003. The Nisqually Tribe announced plans in 2023 for the Quiemuth Resort casino and 350-room hotel next to Lacey Gateway.

The whole city is inside North Thurston Public Schools, with North Thurston, River Ridge and Timberline high schools and Chinook, Komachin, Nisqually and Salish middle schools. Saint Martin's University, founded in 1895, is in Lacey, and South Puget Sound Community College has a branch campus here. Providence St. Peter Hospital, the county's largest at 372 beds, sits just northwest of the city.

The Thurston County Treasurer explains what happens when a payment is missed:

  • If the first half is not paid by April 30, the whole year's tax is treated as late and interest runs on the full amount.
  • A 3 percent penalty may be added on June 1 and another 8 percent on December 1.
  • The county does not grant extensions for hardship, and a late payment must include the added charges or it is returned.
  • Real property is not sold for unpaid tax until the taxes are three full years delinquent, and a payment plan is available for delinquent prior-year taxes.

Pay at the Treasurer's office, 3000 Pacific Ave SE, Suite 130, Olympia, or call 360-786-5550. If your lender pays your taxes, the county sends a postcard each February, but the owner remains legally responsible. Clear any unpaid balance before you list, since a title company will find it.

Washington real estate excise tax falls on the seller in the usual case, and the Department of Revenue says the buyer becomes responsible when the seller does not pay it. The tax is due to the county treasurer on the sale date, and the deed and affidavit go to the treasurer, not to the Department of Revenue. The state rate is graduated, and a city local rate is added; RCW 82.46.010 authorizes city excise taxes within a statutory cap. The department also lists an interest rate of 6 percent for 2026 on late excise tax.

Ask the Thurston County Treasurer or your escrow officer for the exact tax on your price. On a $457,100 sale, the state portion at 1.1 percent would come to about $5,028 under the first graduated slice, though thresholds change on January 1, 2027, so rely on the escrow figure.

Under RCW 64.06.020, the seller of improved residential property delivers a completed disclosure form unless the buyer waived it or the sale is exempt. The form is based on what the seller actually knows and asks about the roof, drainage, plumbing, sewer or septic, and environmental items such as lead-based paint, asbestos and fuel tanks.

After delivery the buyer has three business days to rescind unless the contract says otherwise in writing. Lacey sellers with a house served by a septic system should answer the on-site sewage questions carefully, since they cover tanks, drainfields and whether fixtures connect to the system.

Do Lacey's rental rules affect a sale?

A Lacey business license is required to operate a business in the city, and it is applied for through the state Department of Revenue by adding a City of Lacey endorsement to a state registration. The city also requires annual registration of any complex with five or more rental dwelling units. The city describes that program for complexes of that size, so ask the city whether anything else applies to a single rented house.

Work that changes how a building is used needs a city permit under the construction permit rules, and applications go through the city's online portal. If a buyer wants to convert part of the house, open permits or unpermitted work can slow the closing, so ask the city what is on record for your address before you sign a contract.

A cash sale can close in the time it takes to complete title work and choose a closing date. A financed sale adds appraisal and lender steps, and a listing adds showing time.

What is the Thurston County property tax deadline?

The first half is due April 30 and the second half October 31, with a weekend due date moving to the following Monday. The next first-half deadline is April 30, 2027.

Can I sell my Lacey house if I am behind on property taxes?

Yes, but the balance and added interest or penalties are paid from the proceeds or before closing. Thurston County does not allow hardship extensions, though it offers payment plans for delinquent prior-year taxes.

Does Lacey require a rental inspection before I sell a rented house?

The city's rental registration program covers complexes with five or more rental units, and rental activity needs a business license. Ask the city whether anything else applies to a single rented house.

Who must sign the seller disclosure in Lacey?

The seller completes the form and dates and signs each page. The buyer has three business days after delivery to rescind unless the parties agreed otherwise in writing.

What should a seller know about Olympia, Washington?

Olympia is the capital of Washington and the county seat of Thurston County. It sits at the southern end of Puget Sound on Budd Inlet, about 47 miles southwest of Seattle, and shares borders with Lacey and Tumwater. The Census Bureau estimates 56,724 residents as of July 1, 2025, which is 2.4% above the April 2020 estimates base.

Much of downtown sits on reclaimed land, and the Deschutes River was dammed in 1951 to form Capitol Lake. The state approved removing that dam in late 2022. A house near the water or on fill can draw questions about soil and drainage, so gather any past inspection reports before you list.

Olympia has a council-manager government and its own permit center at City Hall, 601 4th Avenue E. Most sellers deal with the city only if they have open permits, a rental, or a lot that could take more housing. The sections below cover those points, then the state and county steps every Olympia sale goes through.

How do Olympia's housing numbers compare?

Census QuickFacts gives a quick picture of who lives in Olympia and what homes are worth. The figures below come from the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 survey period unless noted.
